title: Sorting fundamentals and comparison contracts
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its constraints.
Trace the example and reason about its data flow.
Identify complexity, boundary or safety considerations.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Sorting arranges elements according to a comparison rule. Algorithms differ in time complexity, extra storage, stability and behaviour on nearly sorted input. A comparator must define a consistent ordering for the data.
understand.whyItMatters: Sorting enables efficient searching and grouping, but an inconsistent comparison function can make results incorrect or violate library function requirements.
understand.analogy: Treat an algorithm or data structure as a set of operations that must preserve a clearly stated contract.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace formal complexity analysis, C object rules or algorithm preconditions.

explain.narrative:
Sorting arranges elements according to a comparison rule. Algorithms differ in time complexity, extra storage, stability and behaviour on nearly sorted input. A comparator must define a consistent ordering for the data.

Before implementation, state input constraints, empty-case behaviour, ownership and invariants. Compile with warnings and test representative, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: qsort calls the comparator for elements. The expression (a > b) - (a < b) returns a negative, zero or positive result without risking overflow from subtracting a - b.

practise.guidedTask: Explain why returning a - b from an int comparator can overflow.
practise.independentTask: Sort records by a selected field and define a consistent comparison for equal values.
hints: qsort does not promise a stable ordering for equal elements.
The comparator must not violate transitivity or consistency.
Pass the correct element size and number of elements.
